For certain species in the higher ionization stages, such as Fe III, O II and N II, the intense emission lines that would be detectable in single-shot LIB spectra with the current setup are outside the wavelength range recorded by the spectrometer. Therefore, their relative number densities cannot be derived directly from spectral fitting, even though these values are necessary for calculating the particle O to Fe ratio. The relevance of these higher ionization stages is evident in figure 3. It shows the normalized number densities of Fe I, Fe II, Fe III, O I, O II, O III, N I, N II, and N III as a function of plasma excitation temperature at a constant free electron number density of 5.5 • 10 17 cm −3 . These number densities are obtained using the Saha-Boltzmann equation given in equation (3.7) [35]. At typical plasma excitation temperatures of about 14 000 K, a substantial fraction of O and N are already present in the first ionization stage (O II, N II). Higher states (O III, N III) do not contribute to the total sum for the analyzed plasma conditions. For Fe, the transition from the neutral state (Fe I) to the singly (Fe II) and the doubly ionized states (Fe III) is clearly visible. 

The elemental balance would be strongly biased if only the relative atomic number densities (Fe I, Fe II, O I, N I) derived directly from spectral fitting are considered. For instance, at 14 000 K, about 10 % of O and N atoms are already ionized, which leads to a significant underestimation of the total number densities. The most commonly used approach for the determination of the temperature and the electron density of LIBS plasmas is the Saha-Boltzmann plot, which is based on the previous determination of the electron density via (i) the Stark broadening effect or (ii) the Saha-Boltzmann equation. In the former approach, the measurement of the Stark width of a selected spectral line with a known value of its broadening coefficient is required [11]. In the latter approach, the emission intensity ratio of two lines corresponding to successive ionization states of the same element is employed [12]. In most cases, the H α Balmer emission line (at λ α = 656.28 nm) is selected as this line is, in general, well-isolated, free of self-absorption, and has a considerably larger Stark broadening than any other element. Although a proper measurement of the H α line profile can be achieved even by using a spectrometer with a low spectral resolution, this line was not available for the spectral range of our system. Moreover, the spectral resolution of the spectrometer was about 0.18 nm, which is larger than the expected Stark widths of the other elements detected (~0.01 nm), thus preventing the use of the Stark broadening approach to determine the electron density. Electron density refers to the quantity of free electrons within a given volume. Determining electron density is possible via various reliable methods, such as Thomson scattering, microwave, and plasma spectroscopy. Within this laboratory context, utilizing the linear Stark broadening of spectral lines proves to be a reliable technique for determining electron density. The primary factors contributing to line broadening in LIBS plasmas are the Stark effect and Doppler width. The Doppler width is solely determined by the emitting species atomic mass and temperature. This broadening is not considered significant in this experiment because the hydrogen line's Doppler width employed typically falls within the range of 0.04 to 0.07 nm. Considered a form of pressure broadening, the Stark effect is caused by the interaction between adjacent particles and radiators. These interactions occur in plasmas due to ion collisions and, to a lesser degree, electron collisions. The primary factor contributing to the broadening of the hydrogen line is attributed to the Stark effect [17].
